headline: RM2.27 Billion, 25 Charges, One Verdict, and the Reform Bill Still Unpassed
context: Najib Razak was convicted on all 25 charges over RM2.27 billion from 1MDB on 26 December 2025. The court imposed 15 years jail and an RM11.38 billion fine. Malaysia has paid RM42 billion on 1MDB debt; Anwar put the balance at about RM13 billion.

changes.summary: Correction: The debt still owed is RM24.46 billion; RM42 billion is what has been paid in debt service. Stated the fine as RM11.3879 billion and dated the draft political financing bill to July 2022.

Correction: Earlier editions said RM24.46 billion of 1MDB debt was still owed and called a Putrajaya rally a response to the verdict; Anwar told Parliament in December 2025 that about RM13 billion was left to settle, and the rally took place in January 2025, a year before the verdict.

cards.big: Najib was convicted on all 25 charges and appealed within days; UMNO sought his pardon. Lost in both: the RM42 billion Malaysia has paid on 1MDB debt.
cards.sub: The court rejected four Saudi donation letters as forgeries. The conviction did not address the patronage structures that produced the case.

cards.big: The judge declared four Saudi donation letters forgeries. Najib was convicted on all 25 charges.
cards.sub: The fine was RM11.38 billion for the four abuse-of-power charges (5× gratification). Appeal filed days after the 26 December verdict.

cards.big: Malaysia has paid about RM42 billion servicing 1MDB-linked debt. In December 2025 Anwar told Parliament about RM13 billion was left to settle.
cards.sub: Anwar said 1MDB is still the government's biggest debt.

cards.big: Political-financing reform remains unpassed. On 26 October 2026 the bill's policy recommendations were still bound for a select committee, then Cabinet.
cards.sub: After the verdict, C4's Cynthia Gabriel urged the government to pass a proposed law regulating political financing.

cards.big: The conviction closes a case. It does not change the financing rules that produced it.
Connected elites across the political spectrum benefit from the absence of donor-disclosure law. Vulnerable households carry the longer-term fiscal cost.
